title: Securing Controlled Stock, Reporting Theft or Loss, and Disposing of It Lawfully
subtopic: Physical and personnel security of the controlled stock, the theft-or-loss report, and the permitted disposal routes with their destruction standard and records
learning_objectives: State what 247 CMR 9.21 requires of a Massachusetts pharmacy: where controlled substances are stored, the three permitted arrangements for Schedules II through V, and what the alarm, camera and barrier paragraphs demand.
Say who is responsible for pharmacy security and access to the prescription area, and who may and may not make entries in or adjustments to the Schedule II perpetual inventory.
Identify who 105 CMR 700.005(B) binds before applying it, and state the federal hiring bar in 21 CFR 1301.76(a) that reaches every DEA-registered pharmacy.
Separate a discrepancy found on a count from a reportable event, and name the two federal clocks that both start at discovery of a theft or significant loss.

List the factors 21 CFR 1301.76(b) tells a registrant to weigh in judging whether a loss is significant, and say which sentences of the non-practitioner paragraph 21 CFR 1301.74(c) do not travel with it.

Lay the Massachusetts theft and loss routes beside the federal one: the seven-day Board report with a copy of the DEA Form 106 under 247 CMR 20.03(7), the simultaneous police copies under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 15, and the 24-hour Drug Control Program report under 105 CMR 700.008.
Name the ways 21 CFR 1317.05(a) allows a practitioner to dispose of controlled substances in its own inventory, and identify the route that is written for non-practitioners only.
State the non-retrievable standard in 21 CFR 1317.90 and match each destination in 21 CFR 1317.95 to the two-employee procedure it carries.
Say when a DEA Form 41 is the required record of destruction under 21 CFR 1304.21(e), when it is not, and what separate use 21 CFR 1317.05(a)(4) makes of the same form.
State the reverse distributor's own registration duty, the delivery controls in 21 CFR 1317.15(b), and the 30-calendar-day destruction deadline in 21 CFR 1317.15(d).
Name the order form and record a Schedule II movement out of the pharmacy carries, whether it goes to a reverse distributor or back for return or recall.

orientation.text: Security in a Massachusetts pharmacy is a list of checkable conditions rather than a general aspiration, and 247 CMR 9.21 states them one at a time. All controlled substances are stored within the secured prescription area and in a safe and secure manner. Schedules II through V are stored in a securely locked and substantially constructed cabinet, or a similarly secured storage area, or dispersed throughout the stock of Schedule VI controlled substances in such a manner as to obstruct theft and diversion, so dispersal is a third permitted arrangement rather than a relaxation of the first two. The pharmacy maintains a centrally monitored security system that is able to detect a breach in security and is designed to prevent theft, and activates it when the pharmacy is closed. It maintains surveillance cameras in a manner designed to record theft and diversion of controlled substances, and retains video records for at least 14 days or, in the case of known or suspected theft or diversion, at least two years. A pharmacy located within another retail establishment is secured by a floor to ceiling barrier, securely locked and separately alarmed at all times when the pharmacy is closed. All drug order deliveries containing controlled substances are delivered directly to the pharmacy. None of this switches off for stock the pharmacy no longer wants, because 247 CMR 9.21(10) applies each requirement of the section to controlled substances that are expired, quarantined, or pending reverse distribution.

Who may be near the stock is settled in several places that answer different questions, and the first thing to settle is which of them is addressed to the pharmacy in front of you. 247 CMR 9.21(6) fixes responsibility inside the pharmacy: the pharmacist Manager of Record and the pharmacist on duty are responsible for pharmacy security and shall control access to the prescription area. The perpetual-inventory paragraph narrows that further, providing that an inventory adjustment resulting from a discrepancy is performed only by the pharmacist Manager of Record, or in the Manager of Record's absence by a pharmacist designee who then reports to the Manager of Record, that an unlicensed individual may not make any entry into or adjust the perpetual inventory, and that a certified pharmacy technician may make entries. The hiring question is where a candidate most easily reaches for the wrong sovereign, so read the addressee of each rule before applying it.

105 CMR 700.005(B) is a Department of Public Health rule, and it speaks to applicants and registrants. Registrant is defined in 105 CMR 700.001 as a person who is registered by the Department under M.G.L. c. 94C, and the Department's own registration provision excludes the retail pharmacy: 105 CMR 700.004(A)(1) reaches every person other than a registered retail drug business or wholesale druggist, while M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7(a) requires every pharmacy to register with the Board of Registration in Pharmacy instead. So the personnel provisions of 105 CMR 700.005(B) reach an operator that holds a Department registration, such as a hospital or other health facility registered under 105 CMR 700.004(A)(3), and not a Board-licensed retail pharmacy in that capacity. 247 CMR 9.21(12) shows the same division from the Board's side, sending only an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy to 105 CMR 700.000 for storage and security. What those provisions say, where they apply, is this. All applicants and registrants shall screen before employment new employees who may work in or around areas where controlled substances are handled. Under 105 CMR 700.005(B)(1) the screening is made solely for the purpose of determining whether the prospective employee is a responsible person who can be trusted to work in and around controlled substances, and documentation of the screening is made available to the Commissioner upon request rather than filed in advance. Under 105 CMR 700.005(B)(2) no registrant shall knowingly employ any agent or employee who has had an application for registration denied for violation of any law or regulation, or has had their registration revoked for violation of any law or regulation, at any time.

The hiring rule that does bind every DEA-registered pharmacy is federal. Under 21 CFR 1301.76(a) the registrant shall not employ, as an agent or employee who has access to controlled substances, any person who has been convicted of a felony offense relating to controlled substances, or who at any time had an application for registration with DEA denied, had a DEA registration revoked, or has surrendered a DEA registration for cause, which the paragraph defines as a surrender in lieu of or as a consequence of a federal or state administrative, civil or criminal action arising from an investigation of that individual's handling of controlled substances. Compare it with the Department rule rather than merging the two. The federal bar is wider in what it catches, because it adds felony drug convictions and surrenders for cause. It is narrower in who it catches, because it reaches an agent or employee who has access to controlled substances, so what the person is actually allowed to touch is part of the federal test in a way it is not part of the Department's. And neither rule is written without any route out: 105 CMR 700.140 lets the Commissioner waive one or more requirements imposed through 105 CMR 700.000 on stated findings, and 21 CFR 1307.03 lets any person apply in writing to DEA for an exception to any provision of the chapter, which the Administrator may grant in his discretion.

A missing quantity is not automatically a reportable event, and the sequence matters. 247 CMR 9.21(8)(c) requires a pharmacy to reconcile the perpetual inventory for each Schedule II controlled substance at least once every ten days by performing an accurate physical count of inventory on hand and comparing it with the perpetual inventory, and it then puts the next step on one person: the Manager of Record shall investigate any discrepancy and report any significant loss or suspected theft in accordance with federal and state requirements. The federal requirement for a pharmacy sits in 21 CFR 1301.76(b), the paragraph written for practitioners, because 21 U.S.C. 802(21) names a pharmacy in the definition of practitioner; the parallel paragraph 21 CFR 1301.74(c) is written for non-practitioners. Under 1301.76(b) the registrant shall notify the Field Division Office of the Administration in its area, in writing, of the theft or significant loss of any controlled substances within one business day of discovery, and must also file a complete and accurate DEA Form 106 with the Administration through DEA's Diversion Control Division secure network application within 45 days after discovery. Those are two duties running on two clocks, not one duty with a long deadline. Significance is judged rather than counted, against the factors the paragraph supplies: the actual quantity lost in relation to the type of business, the specific substances lost, whether the loss can be associated with access by specific individuals or attributed to unique activities, a pattern of losses over a specific time period with whether they appear random and the results of efforts taken to resolve them, and, if known, whether the substances are likely candidates for diversion together with local trends and other indicators of diversion potential.

Two sentences that candidates attach to a pharmacy belong to the non-practitioner paragraph instead, and the difference is worth holding. 21 CFR 1301.74(c) is the paragraph that says expressly that thefts and significant losses must be reported whether or not the controlled substances are subsequently recovered or the responsible parties are identified and action taken against them, and it is the paragraph that allocates in-transit losses to the supplier, unless the theft or loss occurs during an import or export transaction. Neither sentence appears in 21 CFR 1301.76(b). What 1301.76 says about goods in transit runs the other way: under 1301.76(d) a retail pharmacy that contracts with a private, common or contract carrier to retrieve filled prescriptions from a central fill pharmacy is itself responsible for reporting in-transit losses on a DEA Form 106 upon discovery. 21 CFR 1301.76(c) adds a bridge worth knowing: whenever a practitioner distributes a controlled substance without being registered as a distributor, as 21 CFR 1307.11, 1317.05 and 1317.10 permit, it must comply with the non-practitioner requirements in 21 CFR 1301.74(a), (b) and (e), which is how the carrier-selection duty reaches a pharmacy sending stock out for disposal.

Massachusetts adds two further routes to the federal one, with their own actors and their own clocks, and the DEA filing answers for none of them. First, 247 CMR 20.03(7) requires a Drug Store pharmacy, sterile compounding pharmacy, complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy or nuclear pharmacy located in Massachusetts to report a theft or loss of a significant amount of controlled substances by submitting to the Board a copy of the Report of Theft or Loss of Controlled Substance and DEA Form 106 within seven days of the theft or significant loss, and to comply where applicable with the reporting requirements of the DEA, the Department and the state and local police. Because the Board wants the Form 106 inside seven days, a Massachusetts pharmacy cannot in practice use the whole federal 45. Second, M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 15 attaches copies to that Form 106: a person registered to dispense who discovers a theft or loss requiring the filing of a DEA Form 106 shall simultaneously file a copy with the police department in the city or town where the theft or loss is alleged to have occurred and with the department of state police, while a person registered to distribute files its copy with the state police. Third, and separately, 105 CMR 700.008 gives a registrant of the Department 24 hours from discovery to report the theft, loss or suspected tampering of any controlled substances to the Drug Control Program within the Department on the form that programme provides or approves. That route binds an operator that holds a Department registration, such as a hospital, and it is what 247 CMR 20.03(7) points a Board-licensed pharmacy at when it says to comply with the Department's requirements where applicable.

Disposal is not ordinary waste handling with extra paperwork. It is a separate scheme with its own part of the regulations, its own permitted destinations and its own witnessing rules, so the answer cannot be reached by asking what is convenient or what the state's waste rules would tolerate. 21 CFR 1317.05(a) opens with a closed list: a registered practitioner in lawful possession of a controlled substance in its inventory that desires to dispose of that substance shall do so in one of the following ways. Those ways are prompt destruction in accordance with subpart C of part 1317 using an on-site method of destruction; prompt delivery to a reverse distributor's registered location, by common or contract carrier pick-up or by reverse distributor pick-up at the registrant's registered location; prompt delivery, for the purpose of return or recall, to the registered person from whom the substance was obtained, to the registered manufacturer of the substance, or to another registrant the manufacturer has authorized to accept returns or recalls on its behalf; and a request for assistance from the Special Agent in Charge of the Administration in the area in which the practitioner is located. A retail pharmacy is a practitioner for these purposes, because 21 U.S.C. 802(21) names a pharmacy in the definition of practitioner. The route that lets a registrant carry the substances to the destruction site by its own means is written into 21 CFR 1317.05(b) for non-practitioners, and so is not on the practitioner's list.

Choosing a destination does not dispose of the ordering paperwork, and this is the gap a Schedule II disposal most often leaves. 21 CFR 1305.03 requires either a DEA Form 222 or its electronic equivalent for each distribution of a Schedule I or II controlled substance, and its exception for distributions to reverse distributors is written for collectors and law enforcement rather than for a pharmacy emptying its own shelf. So sending expired Schedule II stock to a reverse distributor is a distribution that runs on an order form. The same is true of the return-or-recall route by its own provision: 21 CFR 1317.10(b) requires each registrant that delivers a Schedule I or II controlled substance for the purpose of return or recall to use an order form in the manner described in part 1305, and 21 CFR 1317.10(a) requires a record of each return or recall transaction. On those movements the pharmacy is the party filling the order rather than placing it, so the federal record it keeps is the original of the form under 21 CFR 1305.17(b), maintained separately from all other records for two years, and, because a pharmacy does not report to ARCOS, a copy of that original goes to DEA at the close of the month under 21 CFR 1305.13(d). None of that displaces the Massachusetts record: 247 CMR 9.21(9) still requires an accurate record of all controlled substances returned to a reverse distributor or disposed of, including proper DEA forms in the case of Schedule II.

Whichever route is chosen, the destruction standard and the record are fixed. 21 CFR 1317.90 requires all controlled substances to be destroyed by a registrant, or caused to be destroyed by a registrant under 21 CFR 1317.95(c), to be destroyed in compliance with applicable Federal, State, tribal and local laws and regulations and to be rendered non-retrievable. Where multiple controlled substances are comingled the method must be sufficient to render all of them non-retrievable, and where the substances collected for destruction are unknown but may reasonably include controlled substances the method must be sufficient to render non-retrievable any controlled substance likely to be present. Non-retrievable is a defined term for the purposes of the disposal part: the substance's physical or chemical condition or state is permanently altered through irreversible means, so that it is unavailable and unusable for all practical purposes and cannot be transformed back into a controlled substance or a controlled substance analogue. 21 CFR 1317.95 then attaches two employees to every destination, and 21 CFR 1304.21(e) attaches the record to only two of them: any registered person that destroys a controlled substance under 21 CFR 1317.95(d), or causes the destruction of a controlled substance under 21 CFR 1317.95(c), shall maintain a record of destruction on a DEA Form 41 that is complete and accurate and includes the name and signature of the two employees who witnessed the destruction. Massachusetts layers its own record on top: 247 CMR 9.21(9) requires a pharmacy to maintain an accurate record of all controlled substances returned to a reverse distributor or disposed of in accordance with state and federal laws and regulations, including proper DEA forms in the case of Schedule II controlled substances.

comparison_tables.title: A theft or loss beside a planned disposal: trigger, first act, form, recipient, clock
columns: Theft or significant loss of controlled substances
Planned disposal of unwanted controlled stock

cells: What starts it

Discovery of a theft or significant loss of any controlled substances; in a Massachusetts pharmacy the discovery commonly comes out of the Schedule II reconciliation required at least once every ten days
A decision by the registrant that it desires to dispose of a controlled substance in its inventory, typically stock that is expired, quarantined or otherwise unwanted
The first act and its clock
Written notice to the Field Division Office of the Administration in the registrant's area within one business day of discovery, under 21 CFR 1301.76(b)
No notice clock; 21 CFR 1317.05(a) requires the chosen route to be taken promptly, and only the request for assistance under 21 CFR 1317.05(a)(4) brings the Administration in beforehand
The form

A complete and accurate DEA Form 106, a copy of which also goes to the Board with the Report of Theft or Loss of Controlled Substance and, simultaneously with the federal filing, to the local and state police
A DEA Form 41 where 21 CFR 1304.21(e) applies, and one copy of a DEA Form 41 listing the substances where the practitioner asks the Special Agent in Charge for assistance under 21 CFR 1317.05(a)(4)
Who receives it, and when

The Administration, through DEA's Diversion Control Division secure network application, within 45 days after discovery; the Board within seven days of the theft or significant loss; the local and state police simultaneously with the Form 106
The Form 41 under 21 CFR 1304.21(e) is a record the registrant maintains rather than a filing; the Special Agent in Charge receives a copy only on a 21 CFR 1317.05(a)(4) request
Does anything later cancel the duty

Nothing in 21 CFR 1301.76(b) releases the duty once discovery has occurred, and the non-practitioner paragraph 21 CFR 1301.74(c) says in terms that thefts and significant losses are reported whether or not the substances are subsequently recovered or the responsible parties identified
The question does not arise, because nothing is missing; the live question is which permitted destination the stock goes to and which procedure that destination carries
The Department's separate route

A registrant of the Department, such as a hospital, reports theft, loss or suspected tampering to the Drug Control Program within 24 hours of discovery on that programme's form; 247 CMR 20.03(7) also tells a Board-licensed pharmacy to comply with the Department's requirements where applicable
Not engaged: a planned disposal is not a theft, a loss or suspected tampering
What the Massachusetts side adds

The Manager of Record investigates any discrepancy and reports any significant loss or suspected theft in accordance with federal and state requirements, and video records are retained at least two years where theft or diversion is known or suspected

An accurate record of all controlled substances returned to a reverse distributor or disposed of, including proper DEA forms in the case of Schedule II, while every security requirement continues to apply to stock that is expired, quarantined or pending reverse distribution

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts pharmacy runs its ten-day Schedule II reconciliation and finds 40 tablets of one product on hand against a perpetual-inventory balance of 70. A technician offers to correct the record to match the count so that the next reconciliation starts clean, and the pharmacist on duty suggests waiting until month end to see whether the numbers settle before telling anyone.
steps: Separate the count from the conclusion. 247 CMR 9.21(8)(c) requires the reconciliation at least once every ten days and then requires the Manager of Record to investigate any discrepancy, so the count triggers an investigation rather than itself establishing a loss.

Fix who may touch the record. 247 CMR 9.21(8) permits an inventory adjustment resulting from a discrepancy to be performed only by the pharmacist Manager of Record, or by a pharmacist designee in the Manager of Record's absence who then reports to the Manager of Record, and it bars an unlicensed individual from making any entry into or adjusting the perpetual inventory.

Judge significance against the factors 21 CFR 1301.76(b) supplies rather than against a threshold: the actual quantity in relation to the type of business, the specific substance, whether the loss can be associated with access by specific individuals or attributed to unique activities, any pattern over a specific time period with whether the losses appear random and the results of efforts to resolve them, and, if known, the diversion potential of the substance and local trends.

If the investigation establishes a theft or significant loss, start both federal clocks from discovery: written notice to the Field Division Office of the Administration in the registrant's area within one business day, and a complete and accurate DEA Form 106 through DEA's Diversion Control Division secure network application within 45 days.

Add the Massachusetts routes rather than stopping at DEA. 247 CMR 20.03(7) gives the pharmacy seven days from the theft or significant loss to submit to the Board a copy of the Report of Theft or Loss of Controlled Substance and the DEA Form 106, which in practice pulls the Form 106 well inside the federal 45 days.

Send the police copies with the federal filing. Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 15 a person registered to dispense who must file a DEA Form 106 shall simultaneously file a copy with the police department in the city or town where the theft or loss is alleged to have occurred and with the department of state police.

Preserve the evidence the state rule expects to exist. 247 CMR 9.21(4) requires video records to be retained for at least two years where theft or diversion is known or suspected, rather than the ordinary 14 days.
worked_examples.resolution: The Manager of Record investigates, the technician does not adjust the record, and if the investigation establishes a theft or significant loss four things follow from discovery: the one-business-day DEA notice, the Form 106, the Board's seven-day report carrying a copy of that Form 106, and the simultaneous police copies. The error the scenario invites is treating an inventory adjustment as the response to a discrepancy, which destroys the evidence the investigation needs; the second is letting a wait-and-see period run against a clock the regulation starts at discovery rather than at proof; the third is answering the whole question with the DEA filing and leaving the Board and the police unserved.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacy has expired Schedule II and Schedule IV stock sitting in a quarantine bin on an open shelf, waiting for the reverse distributor's next pick-up. A technician has already filled out a DEA Form 41 for the bin so the paperwork will be ready, and an intern asks whether the bin still has to sit inside the secured storage now that the drugs can no longer be dispensed.
steps: Name the route. Delivery to a reverse distributor's registered location, by common or contract carrier pick-up or by reverse distributor pick-up at the pharmacy's registered location, is one of the ways 21 CFR 1317.05(a) allows a practitioner to dispose of inventory.

Check the recipient's status rather than its business description. 21 CFR 1317.15(a) requires any person that reverse distributes a controlled substance to be registered with the Administration as a reverse distributor unless exempted by law or otherwise authorized.

Apply 21 CFR 1317.95 to the hand-over itself. A transfer to a person registered or authorized to accept the substances for destruction falls under paragraph (a), so two employees of the transferring registrant load and unload, or observe the loading and unloading, until the transfer is complete.

Ask what 21 CFR 1304.21(e) actually attaches the Form 41 to. It is the record for a registered person that destroys a controlled substance under 21 CFR 1317.95(d) or causes destruction under 21 CFR 1317.95(c); handing stock to a reverse distributor is neither, so the pharmacy destroys nothing and creates no such record.

Find the record that the Schedule II half of the bin does need. 21 CFR 1305.03 requires a DEA Form 222 or electronic order for each distribution of a Schedule I or II controlled substance, and its exception for distributions to reverse distributors is written for collectors and law enforcement, so the Schedule II stock moves on an order form while the Schedule IV stock does not.

Place that form correctly. On this movement the pharmacy fills the order rather than placing it, so it retains the original under 21 CFR 1305.17(b), separately from all other records, and, not reporting to ARCOS, submits a copy to DEA at the close of the month under 21 CFR 1305.13(d).

Answer the intern from 247 CMR 9.21(10), which applies each requirement of the section to controlled substances that are expired, quarantined, or pending reverse distribution, so the bin belongs inside the security the section requires.

Note where the duty travels next. 21 CFR 1317.15(d) requires the reverse distributor to destroy or cause the destruction of any controlled substance received for the purpose of destruction no later than 30 calendar days after receipt.
worked_examples.resolution: The bin goes back into secured storage, the Schedule II stock moves on a DEA Form 222 or electronic order whose original the pharmacy keeps, the pick-up follows the two-employee transfer procedure, and the pharmacy records the transfer under 247 CMR 9.21(9) rather than on a Form 41. The error the scenario invites is treating the DEA Form 41 as a receipt for anything that leaves the pharmacy for disposal, when it is a record of destruction; the second is assuming that stock which can no longer be dispensed has passed out of the reach of the security rule; the third is forgetting that a Schedule II hand-over is still a distribution and still needs an order form.

worked_examples.scenario: Two employers in Massachusetts are looking at the same applicant for a stock assistant who will unpack deliveries beside the controlled-substance store. One is a Board-licensed retail Drug Store pharmacy; the other is a hospital that holds a Department of Public Health controlled substance registration. Nine years ago the applicant surrendered his own DEA registration in the face of an investigation into his handling of controlled substances, and he has worked without incident since. Each employer asks whether it may hire him if it documents the history and keeps him away from the controlled-substance store itself.
steps: Take the Department rule first and read its addressee. 105 CMR 700.005(B) binds applicants and registrants, 105 CMR 700.001 defines Registrant as a person registered by the Department under M.G.L. c. 94C, and 105 CMR 700.004(A)(1) excludes a registered retail drug business from Department registration while M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7(a) sends every pharmacy to the Board instead. The hospital is a Department registrant; the retail pharmacy is not.

Apply the Department provisions to the hospital. It screens before employment, because the applicant may work in or around an area where controlled substances are handled; under 105 CMR 700.005(B)(1) that screening is made solely to determine whether he is a responsible person who can be trusted to work in and around controlled substances, and the documentation is produced to the Commissioner on request rather than filed in advance. Then read 105 CMR 700.005(B)(2): its two limbs are a denied application and a revoked registration, and a surrender is neither, so this history does not trigger that bar.

Turn to the rule that binds both employers. 21 CFR 1301.76 states security controls for practitioners, and 21 U.S.C. 802(21) makes both a pharmacy and a hospital practitioners, so paragraph (a) reaches each of them as a DEA registrant. It forbids employing, as an agent or employee who has access to controlled substances, anyone who has surrendered a DEA registration for cause, which the paragraph defines as a surrender in lieu of or as a consequence of an action arising from an investigation of that individual's handling of controlled substances.

Notice that access is part of the federal test. The federal bar reaches an agent or employee who has access to controlled substances, so unlike the Department's flat prohibition on employing the person, a genuine restriction of access is a question the federal wording puts in play rather than an irrelevance.
Give the time element its weight. The federal registration limbs run at any time, so nine clean years do not lift them, and neither rule offers a look-back period as a route out.

Read the remaining routes before concluding that nothing can be done. 21 CFR 1307.03 lets any person apply in writing to DEA for an exception to a provision of the chapter, which the Administrator may grant in his discretion, and 105 CMR 700.140 lets the Commissioner waive a requirement of 105 CMR 700.000 for a Department registrant on findings of undue hardship, no jeopardy to health or safety, acceptable compensating measures and written documentation.

Remember that hiring is not the only access control. 247 CMR 9.21(6) makes the pharmacist Manager of Record and the pharmacist on duty responsible for pharmacy security and requires them to control access to the prescription area, so even a lawful hire does not arrive with unrestricted access.
worked_examples.resolution: Neither employer may put him in a post with access to controlled substances, and the reason is the federal bar in 21 CFR 1301.76(a) rather than the Department provision: a surrender for cause is one of the federal limbs and is not one of the two limbs in 105 CMR 700.005(B)(2). The errors the scenario invites are applying a Department rule to a Board-licensed pharmacy that is not a Department registrant, and treating a restriction of duties as irrelevant when the federal bar is expressly about access.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Where does 247 CMR 9.21 require a pharmacy to store controlled substances, and what are the three permitted arrangements for Schedules II through V?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Within the secured prescription area and in a safe and secure manner. Schedules II through V go in a securely locked and substantially constructed cabinet, or a similarly secured storage area, or dispersed throughout the stock of Schedule VI controlled substances in such a manner as to obstruct theft and diversion.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How long must a Massachusetts pharmacy retain surveillance video records, and what changes the answer?
retrieval_prompts.answer: At least 14 days, and at least two years in the case of known or suspected theft or diversion.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Who is responsible for pharmacy security under 247 CMR 9.21, and who may make entries in or adjustments to the Schedule II perpetual inventory?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The pharmacist Manager of Record and the pharmacist on duty are responsible and control access to the prescription area. A certified pharmacy technician may make entries; an unlicensed individual may not make any entry or adjustment; and an adjustment resulting from a discrepancy is performed only by the Manager of Record, or by a pharmacist designee in the Manager of Record's absence who then reports to the Manager of Record.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Who does 105 CMR 700.005(B) bind, and how do you tell?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Applicants and registrants of the Department. 105 CMR 700.001 defines Registrant as a person registered by the Department under M.G.L. c. 94C, 105 CMR 700.004(A)(1) excludes a registered retail drug business from that registration, and M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7(a) sends every pharmacy to the Board instead. A hospital or other health facility registered under 105 CMR 700.004(A)(3) is bound; a Board-licensed retail pharmacy is not, in that capacity.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Where a 105 CMR 700.005(B) screening is owed, when does it happen, what single purpose does it serve, and where does the documentation go?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Before employment, for new employees who may work in or around areas where controlled substances are handled; solely to determine whether the prospective employee is a responsible person who can be trusted to work in and around controlled substances; and the documentation is made available to the Commissioner upon request.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: State the employment bar in 105 CMR 700.005(B)(2) and the words that decide how long it lasts.
retrieval_prompts.answer: No registrant shall knowingly employ any agent or employee who has had an application for registration denied for violation of any law or regulation, or has had their registration revoked for violation of any law or regulation, at any time. The closing words at any time leave no look-back period.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: State the federal hiring bar that reaches every DEA-registered pharmacy, and the three things it adds to or subtracts from the Department's version.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Under 21 CFR 1301.76(a) a registrant shall not employ, as an agent or employee who has access to controlled substances, anyone convicted of a felony offense relating to controlled substances or who at any time had a DEA application denied, a DEA registration revoked, or a DEA registration surrendered for cause. It adds felony drug convictions and surrenders for cause, and it is confined to employees who have access to controlled substances.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Two clocks start when a theft or significant loss is discovered at a pharmacy. Name each, and name the provision they come from.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Written notice to the Field Division Office of the Administration in the registrant's area within one business day of discovery, and a complete and accurate DEA Form 106 filed with the Administration through DEA's Diversion Control Division secure network application within 45 days after discovery. Both sit in 21 CFR 1301.76(b), the practitioner paragraph, rather than in 21 CFR 1301.74(c).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which two sentences of 21 CFR 1301.74(c) have no counterpart in 21 CFR 1301.76(b)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: That thefts and significant losses must be reported whether or not the controlled substances are subsequently recovered or the responsible parties identified, and the allocation of in-transit losses to the supplier. 21 CFR 1301.76(d) runs the other way for a retail pharmacy that contracts the carrier retrieving filled prescriptions from a central fill pharmacy.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A Massachusetts Drug Store pharmacy has to file a DEA Form 106. What else is owed, to whom, and on what clock?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A copy of the Report of Theft or Loss of Controlled Substance and of the DEA Form 106 to the Board within seven days of the theft or significant loss under 247 CMR 20.03(7), and, simultaneously with the Form 106 filing, a copy to the police department in the city or town where the theft or loss is alleged to have occurred and to the department of state police under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 15.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which theft or loss route runs on 24 hours, who owes it, and what starts it?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 105 CMR 700.008: a registrant of the Department reports theft, loss or suspected tampering of any controlled substances to the Drug Control Program within the Department within 24 hours of discovery, on the form that programme provides or approves. Suspicion of tampering is a trigger in its own right.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A pharmacy sends expired Schedule II stock to a reverse distributor. Which federal instrument does that movement need, and why is the reverse-distributor exception in 21 CFR 1305.03 no answer?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A DEA Form 222 or its electronic equivalent, because the movement is a distribution of a Schedule II controlled substance. The exception in 21 CFR 1305.03(f) covers distributions to reverse distributors by collectors and law enforcement, not a pharmacy disposing of its own inventory.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What does 21 CFR 1317.10 require of a registrant that delivers Schedule II stock for return or recall?
retrieval_prompts.answer: An order form used in the manner described in part 1305, and a record of the return or recall transaction; deliveries may go through a freight forwarding facility operated by the person to whom the substance is being returned only on advance notice and with direct delivery to that person's agent or employee.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name the ways 21 CFR 1317.05(a) allows a practitioner to dispose of a controlled substance in its own inventory.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Prompt on-site destruction in accordance with subpart C of part 1317; prompt delivery to a reverse distributor's registered location; prompt delivery for return or recall to the registered person from whom it was obtained, the registered manufacturer, or another registrant the manufacturer authorized to accept returns or recalls; and a request for assistance from the Special Agent in Charge in the practitioner's area, made by submitting one copy of a DEA Form 41 listing the substances.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What does non-retrievable mean, and what does 21 CFR 1317.90 require where substances are comingled or unidentified?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The substance's physical or chemical condition or state is permanently altered through irreversible means so that it is unavailable and unusable for all practical purposes and cannot be transformed back into a controlled substance or analogue. Where substances are comingled the method must render all of them non-retrievable, and where the substances collected are unknown but may reasonably include controlled substances the method must be sufficient for any controlled substance likely to be present.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which two paragraphs of 21 CFR 1317.95 make a DEA Form 41 the required record, and what must that record contain?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Paragraph (d), on-site destruction, and paragraph (c), causing destruction after transport to a location that is not registered. Under 21 CFR 1304.21(e) the record must be complete and accurate and include the name and signature of the two employees who witnessed the destruction.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How soon must a reverse distributor destroy a controlled substance it received for destruction, and where may a delivery to it be made?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No later than 30 calendar days after receipt. Delivery may be made only to the reverse distributor at its registered location, may not be re-routed to any other location or person once en route regardless of registration status, and must be personally received by an employee of the reverse distributor at the registered location.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which controlled stock does 247 CMR 9.21 stop protecting once it has been set aside for disposal?
retrieval_prompts.answer: None. 247 CMR 9.21(10) applies each requirement of the section to controlled substances that are expired, quarantined, or pending reverse distribution.

quick_review.text: A pharmacy stores all controlled substances within the secured prescription area and in a safe and secure manner, and stores Schedules II through V in a securely locked and substantially constructed cabinet, a similarly secured storage area, or dispersed throughout the stock of Schedule VI controlled substances so as to obstruct theft and diversion.
A centrally monitored security system able to detect a breach in security and designed to prevent theft is maintained and activated when the pharmacy is closed.

Surveillance cameras are maintained in a manner designed to record theft and diversion of controlled substances, and video records are retained at least 14 days, or at least two years in the case of known or suspected theft or diversion.
A pharmacy located within another retail establishment is secured by a floor to ceiling barrier, securely locked and separately alarmed at all times when the pharmacy is closed.
All drug order deliveries containing controlled substances are delivered directly to the pharmacy.
The pharmacist Manager of Record and the pharmacist on duty are responsible for pharmacy security and control access to the prescription area.

The Schedule II perpetual inventory is reconciled at least once every ten days by an accurate physical count compared with the record, and the Manager of Record investigates any discrepancy and reports any significant loss or suspected theft in accordance with federal and state requirements.

105 CMR 700.005(B) is addressed to applicants and registrants of the Department; 105 CMR 700.001 defines Registrant as a person registered by the Department under M.G.L. c. 94C, and 105 CMR 700.004(A)(1) together with M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7(a) leaves a retail drug business registered with the Board rather than with the Department.

Where it applies, screening under 105 CMR 700.005(B) happens before employment, reaches new employees who may work in or around areas where controlled substances are handled, and serves solely to determine whether the prospective employee is a responsible person who can be trusted to work in and around controlled substances.
Documentation of that screening is made available to the Commissioner upon request, which is a duty to produce rather than a duty to file.

No registrant shall knowingly employ any agent or employee who has had an application for registration denied for violation of any law or regulation, or has had their registration revoked for violation of any law or regulation, at any time.

21 CFR 1301.76(a) forbids a registrant to employ, as an agent or employee who has access to controlled substances, anyone convicted of a felony offense relating to controlled substances or who at any time had a DEA application denied, a DEA registration revoked, or a DEA registration surrendered for cause.
A pharmacy is a practitioner under 21 U.S.C. 802(21), which is why its federal security duties sit in 21 CFR 1301.76 rather than in the non-practitioner section 21 CFR 1301.74.

Written notice of the theft or significant loss of any controlled substances goes to the Field Division Office of the Administration in the registrant's area within one business day of discovery, under 21 CFR 1301.76(b).
A complete and accurate DEA Form 106 is filed with the Administration through DEA's Diversion Control Division secure network application within 45 days after discovery of the theft or loss.

Significance is judged against the quantity lost in relation to the type of business, the specific substances lost, association with access by specific individuals or with unique activities, any pattern of losses over a specific time period with whether they appear random and the results of efforts to resolve them, and, if known, diversion candidacy and local trends.

247 CMR 20.03(7) requires a Drug Store pharmacy, sterile compounding pharmacy, complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy or nuclear pharmacy located in Massachusetts to submit to the Board a copy of the Report of Theft or Loss of Controlled Substance and DEA Form 106 within seven days of a theft or significant loss of controlled substances.

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 15 requires a person registered to dispense who must file a DEA Form 106 to file a copy simultaneously with the police department in the city or town where the theft or loss is alleged to have occurred and with the department of state police; a person registered to distribute files with the state police.

105 CMR 700.008 gives a registrant of the Department 24 hours from discovery to report theft, loss or suspected tampering of any controlled substances to the Drug Control Program on the form that programme provides or approves.

A distribution of Schedule I or II stock out of the pharmacy, including a delivery to a reverse distributor, requires a DEA Form 222 or its electronic equivalent, because the 21 CFR 1305.03 exception for distributions to reverse distributors is written for collectors and law enforcement.
21 CFR 1317.10 requires an order form for a Schedule I or II delivery made for the purpose of return or recall, and a record of each return or recall transaction.

21 CFR 1317.05(a) states a closed list of the ways a practitioner may dispose of a controlled substance in its inventory: prompt on-site destruction, prompt delivery to a reverse distributor's registered location, prompt delivery for return or recall, or a request for assistance from the Special Agent in Charge.

Any person that reverse distributes a controlled substance must be registered with the Administration as a reverse distributor unless exempted by law or otherwise authorized, and 21 CFR 1317.15(d) requires it to destroy or cause the destruction of substances received for destruction no later than 30 calendar days after receipt.

Deliveries to a reverse distributor may be made only at its registered location, may not be re-routed once en route regardless of registration status, and must be personally received by an employee of the reverse distributor at that location.

All controlled substances destroyed by a registrant, or caused to be destroyed under 21 CFR 1317.95(c), must be destroyed in compliance with applicable Federal, State, tribal and local laws and regulations and rendered non-retrievable.

Where multiple controlled substances are comingled the method must render all of them non-retrievable, and where the substances collected are unknown but may reasonably include controlled substances the method must be sufficient for any controlled substance likely to be present.
21 CFR 1317.95 requires two employees at every destination, and adds the personal witnessing requirement for destruction under paragraphs (c) and (d).

A registered person that destroys a controlled substance under 21 CFR 1317.95(d), or causes destruction under 21 CFR 1317.95(c), maintains a record of destruction on a DEA Form 41 that is complete and accurate and includes the name and signature of the two employees who witnessed the destruction.

247 CMR 9.21(9) requires an accurate record of all controlled substances returned to a reverse distributor or disposed of in accordance with state and federal laws and regulations, including proper DEA forms in the case of Schedule II controlled substances.

decision_logic.condition: Controlled stock is being put away, locked up or left overnight in a Massachusetts pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Apply 247 CMR 9.21 paragraph by paragraph: the secured prescription area, one of the three permitted arrangements for Schedules II through V, the centrally monitored system activated at closing, cameras with the retention the section sets, and, inside another retail establishment, the floor to ceiling barrier securely locked and separately alarmed.

decision_logic.condition: A new employee will have access to controlled substances at a DEA-registered pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Apply 21 CFR 1301.76(a): do not employ, in a post with access to controlled substances, anyone convicted of a felony offense relating to controlled substances or who at any time had a DEA application denied, a DEA registration revoked, or a DEA registration surrendered for cause.

decision_logic.condition: Someone proposes to apply 105 CMR 700.005(B) to an employer.
decision_logic.action: Ask first whether that employer is a registrant of the Department. A hospital or other health facility registered under 105 CMR 700.004(A)(3) is; a retail drug business licensed and registered by the Board is not, and is reached instead by the federal bar and by the Board's own rules.

decision_logic.condition: A Department registrant is hiring a new employee who may work in or around an area where controlled substances are handled.
decision_logic.action: Screen before employment for trustworthiness around controlled substances, keep the documentation available for the Commissioner on request, and check 105 CMR 700.005(B)(2) before extending an offer, because a denied application or a revoked registration for violation of any law or regulation bars knowing employment at any time.

decision_logic.condition: A bar appears to leave no room and someone asks whether there is any route out.
decision_logic.action: Name the two that exist: 21 CFR 1307.03 lets any person apply in writing to DEA for an exception to a provision of the chapter, which the Administrator may grant in his discretion, and 105 CMR 700.140 lets the Commissioner waive a requirement of 105 CMR 700.000 for a registrant on the four findings it lists. Neither is a right to relief.

decision_logic.condition: A ten-day Schedule II reconciliation, or any other count, produces a discrepancy.
decision_logic.action: Have the Manager of Record investigate before anyone adjusts the record, and let only the Manager of Record, or a pharmacist designee in the Manager of Record's absence, make an adjustment arising from that discrepancy.

decision_logic.condition: The investigation establishes a theft or significant loss of controlled substances.
decision_logic.action: Send written notice to the Field Division Office of the Administration in the registrant's area within one business day of discovery, and file a complete and accurate DEA Form 106 through DEA's Diversion Control Division secure network application within 45 days after discovery; later recovery of the substances does not lift the duty.

decision_logic.condition: The pharmacy establishing that theft or significant loss is located in Massachusetts.
decision_logic.action: Run the state routes alongside the federal one: submit a copy of the Report of Theft or Loss of Controlled Substance and the DEA Form 106 to the Board within seven days of the theft or significant loss, which means the Form 106 has to be completed well inside the federal period, and file a copy of that Form 106 simultaneously with the local police department and the department of state police.

decision_logic.condition: The operator discovering the theft, loss or suspected tampering holds a Department of Public Health controlled substance registration, such as a hospital.
decision_logic.action: Add the 24-hour report to the Drug Control Program within the Department on its own form, measured from discovery, and remember that suspected tampering triggers it without any confirmed shortfall.

decision_logic.condition: Schedule I or II stock is leaving the pharmacy for a reverse distributor, a return or a recall.
decision_logic.action: Put the movement on a DEA Form 222 or electronic order, keep the original of the form the pharmacy filled and the record 21 CFR 1317.10(a) requires for a return or recall, and keep the Massachusetts record 247 CMR 9.21(9) requires as well.

decision_logic.condition: Stock is expired, quarantined or otherwise unwanted and has to leave the pharmacy's usable inventory.
decision_logic.action: Pick one of the routes 21 CFR 1317.05(a) lists for a practitioner and act promptly; do not invent a route, and do not treat transport by the pharmacy's own means to a destruction site as one of them.

decision_logic.condition: A vendor offers to collect unwanted controlled stock for disposal.
decision_logic.action: Confirm the vendor is registered with the Administration as a reverse distributor, deliver only to its registered location by an authorized pick-up or carrier, and expect it to destroy or cause the destruction of the substances no later than 30 calendar days after receipt.

decision_logic.condition: The pharmacy itself will destroy controlled substances rather than transfer them.
decision_logic.action: Render them non-retrievable in compliance with applicable Federal, State, tribal and local laws and regulations, and run the two-employee procedure 21 CFR 1317.95 attaches to the destination, including personal witnessing of the destruction under paragraphs (c) and (d).

decision_logic.condition: The destruction or the transfer is finished and someone asks which record to create.
decision_logic.action: Create a DEA Form 41 only where 21 CFR 1304.21(e) requires it, namely destruction under 21 CFR 1317.95(d) or causing destruction under 21 CFR 1317.95(c), and in either case record the name and signature of the two employees who witnessed the destruction.

decision_logic.condition: The stock being disposed of includes Schedule II product, and the pharmacy is in Massachusetts.
decision_logic.action: Keep the accurate record 247 CMR 9.21(9) requires of all controlled substances returned to a reverse distributor or disposed of, including the proper DEA forms for Schedule II, and keep the stock inside the section's security until it leaves.

ma_vs_federal.text: The Massachusetts storage rule is written for a pharmacy and is more specific than a general security duty: 247 CMR 9.21 names the secured prescription area, the three permitted arrangements for Schedules II through V, a centrally monitored system activated at closing, cameras with a defined retention period, and a floor to ceiling barrier for a pharmacy inside another retail establishment.

The federal theft-or-loss duty runs to the Administration under 21 CFR 1301.76(b), and 247 CMR 9.21(8)(c) routes the same event through the Manager of Record, who investigates any discrepancy and reports any significant loss or suspected theft in accordance with federal and state requirements. The state requirements that sentence points at are real ones of their own, not merely a reference back to the federal rule.

Three Massachusetts routes sit alongside the federal filing, and each has its own actor and clock: the Board report within seven days of the theft or significant loss carrying a copy of the DEA Form 106 under 247 CMR 20.03(7), the simultaneous police copies under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 15, and the Department's 24-hour report to the Drug Control Program under 105 CMR 700.008, which binds an operator holding a Department registration.

The seven-day Board report is the practical constraint on the federal 45-day period, because 247 CMR 20.03(7) requires the copy of the DEA Form 106 to reach the Board within seven days, so a Massachusetts pharmacy cannot use the whole federal window.

The two hiring bars come from different sovereigns and different registers. 21 CFR 1301.76(a) binds every DEA registrant but only as to employees with access to controlled substances, while 105 CMR 700.005(B)(2) binds registrants of the Department and reaches employment as such.

Disposal records stack rather than substitute. The federal record of destruction is the DEA Form 41 required by 21 CFR 1304.21(e), while 247 CMR 9.21(9) separately requires an accurate record of all controlled substances returned to a reverse distributor or disposed of, including proper DEA forms in the case of Schedule II controlled substances.

The statute behind that stacking is M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 15, whose first paragraph requires registered persons to keep records and maintain inventories in conformance with the federal record-keeping and inventory requirements and with any additional rules the Board promulgates for a retail drug business. It is the same section whose second paragraph attaches the police copies to a DEA Form 106, so one provision supplies both the Board's power to add a record like 247 CMR 9.21(9) and the police leg of a theft or loss response.

Federal law decides where unwanted stock may go, and Massachusetts decides how it is held until it goes: 21 CFR 1317.05(a) fixes the practitioner's routes, while 247 CMR 9.21(10) applies every security requirement of the section to controlled substances that are expired, quarantined, or pending reverse distribution.

The Massachusetts personnel bar is a state-law hiring prohibition addressed to registrants of the Department under 105 CMR 700.005(B)(2). The separate duty in 105 CMR 700.005(B)(1) to make screening documentation available to the Commissioner on request is a production duty rather than an advance filing, and the regulation does not make it the mechanism by which the bar itself is enforced.

Disposal paperwork stacks across sovereigns too: the federal side supplies the order form for a Schedule II movement and, where destruction occurs, the DEA Form 41, while 247 CMR 9.21(9) adds the Massachusetts record of everything returned to a reverse distributor or disposed of.

exceptions.text: 247 CMR 9.21(11) provides that the requirements of 247 CMR 9.21 do not apply to non-resident pharmacies.
247 CMR 9.21(12) sends an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy to a different source, requiring it to store and secure controlled substances in accordance with 105 CMR 700.000.

Dispersal is the alternative built into 247 CMR 9.21(2): Schedules II through V need not sit in a cabinet if they are dispersed throughout the stock of Schedule VI controlled substances in such a manner as to obstruct theft and diversion.

105 CMR 700.005(B)(2) states no look-back period and no cure of its own, but it is not beyond reach: 105 CMR 700.140 lets the Commissioner waive one or more requirements imposed through 105 CMR 700.000 on findings of undue hardship, no jeopardy to health or safety, compensating measures acceptable to the Commissioner, and written documentation from the registrant.

The federal bar in 21 CFR 1301.76(a) likewise states no exception in its own words, but 21 CFR 1307.03 lets any person apply in writing to DEA for an exception to any provision of the chapter, which the Administrator may grant in his discretion and is never required to grant.

The allocation of in-transit losses to the supplier belongs to the non-practitioner paragraph 21 CFR 1301.74(c), and does not travel to a pharmacy under 21 CFR 1301.76. For a practitioner the allocation runs the other way in one case: under 21 CFR 1301.76(d) a retail pharmacy that contracts a carrier to retrieve filled prescriptions from a central fill pharmacy reports the in-transit loss itself on a DEA Form 106.

The seven-day Board theft or loss report carries its own limits in its own words: 247 CMR 20.03(7) names a Drug Store pharmacy, sterile compounding pharmacy, complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy and nuclear pharmacy located in Massachusetts, and asks for compliance with the DEA, Department and state and local police requirements only where applicable.

21 CFR 1304.21(e) carves out one destruction from the Form 41 requirement: a controlled substance dispensed by a practitioner for immediate administration at the practitioner's registered location that is not fully exhausted is recorded under the ordinary dispensing-record provision instead.

21 CFR 1317.05(a)(5) allows a standing arrangement where a practitioner is required regularly to dispose of controlled substances: the Special Agent in Charge may authorize disposal without a prior application in each instance, on the condition that the practitioner keeps records of the disposals and files periodic reports summarising them, and may attach further conditions.

timing_deadlines.event: Written notice of a theft or significant loss of controlled substances
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within one business day of discovery of the theft or loss
timing_deadlines.consequence: Notice goes in writing to the Field Division Office of the Administration in the registrant's area under 21 CFR 1301.76(b), and the duty does not wait for the investigation to finish.

timing_deadlines.event: Filing the DEA Form 106 for that theft or loss
timing_deadlines.consequence: A complete and accurate Form 106 is filed with the Administration through DEA's Diversion Control Division secure network application; this is a second duty, not an extension of the first.

timing_deadlines.event: Board report of a theft or loss of a significant amount of controlled substances by a Massachusetts pharmacy
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within seven days of such theft or significant loss
timing_deadlines.consequence: A copy of the Report of Theft or Loss of Controlled Substance and of the DEA Form 106 goes to the Board, which means the Form 106 has to be produced well inside the federal 45 days.

timing_deadlines.event: Police copies of a DEA Form 106 filed by a person registered to dispense
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Simultaneously with the filing of the DEA Form 106
timing_deadlines.consequence: A copy goes to the police department in the city or town where the theft or loss is alleged to have occurred and to the department of state police, so the copies have no clock independent of the federal filing.

timing_deadlines.event: Department report of theft, loss or suspected tampering by a registrant of the Department
timing_deadlines.consequence: The report goes to the Drug Control Program within the Department on the form it provides or approves, and suspected tampering starts the period without any confirmed shortfall.

timing_deadlines.event: Reporting an in-transit loss of filled prescriptions retrieved from a central fill pharmacy under a carrier contracted by the retail pharmacy
timing_deadlines.consequence: The retail pharmacy reports it by use of a DEA Form 106 under 21 CFR 1301.76(d); the supplier allocation in 21 CFR 1301.74(c) is the non-practitioner rule and does not put this duty elsewhere.

timing_deadlines.event: Reconciling the Schedule II perpetual inventory
timing_deadlines.timeframe: At least once every ten days
timing_deadlines.consequence: An accurate physical count of inventory on hand is compared with the perpetual inventory, and any discrepancy goes to the Manager of Record to investigate.
Ordinary retention for cameras maintained in a manner designed to record theft and diversion of controlled substances.

timing_deadlines.event: Retention of surveillance video where theft or diversion is known or suspected
timing_deadlines.consequence: The longer period attaches to the same recordings once theft or diversion is known or suspected, so a decision to delete on the ordinary schedule can destroy the evidence the state rule expects to survive.

timing_deadlines.event: Activation of the pharmacy's centrally monitored security system
timing_deadlines.consequence: A pharmacy inside another retail establishment must in addition be securely locked and separately alarmed at all times when the pharmacy is closed.

timing_deadlines.event: Screening a prospective employee who may work in or around areas where controlled substances are handled
timing_deadlines.consequence: The screening is a condition of hiring rather than an onboarding step, and its documentation must be available to the Commissioner upon request.

timing_deadlines.event: Duration of the bar on knowingly employing a person whose application was denied or whose registration was revoked for violation of any law or regulation
timing_deadlines.timeframe: At any time, with no look-back period
timing_deadlines.consequence: The passage of incident-free years does not lift the bar, and no documentation, restriction of duties or notification is offered as a substitute.

timing_deadlines.event: Destruction by a reverse distributor of substances received for the purpose of destruction
timing_deadlines.timeframe: No later than 30 calendar days after receipt
timing_deadlines.consequence: The reverse distributor destroys or causes the destruction of the substances within that period, having stored them under the security controls in parts 1301 and 1317 in the meantime.

timing_deadlines.event: Acting on a decision to dispose of controlled substances in a practitioner's inventory
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Promptly, in the terms 21 CFR 1317.05(a) uses for each route
timing_deadlines.consequence: Destruction, delivery to a reverse distributor and delivery for return or recall are each required to be prompt, so unwanted stock is not left to accumulate under the security rules indefinitely.

forms_records.text: DEA Form 106 is the theft-or-loss filing: complete and accurate, submitted to the Administration through DEA's Diversion Control Division secure network application within 45 days after discovery, and preceded by written notice to the Field Division Office within one business day.

The one-business-day notice is itself a written record, addressed to the Field Division Office of the Administration in the registrant's area; it is the federal leg of the response, and the Massachusetts reports are separate instruments sent elsewhere.

The same DEA Form 106 does double duty in Massachusetts: a copy goes to the Board with the Report of Theft or Loss of Controlled Substance within seven days of the theft or significant loss, and a copy goes simultaneously to the local police department and the department of state police.

The Department's route has its own instrument: the form the Drug Control Program provides or approves, submitted within 24 hours of discovery, so a copy of the DEA Form 106 is not what that regulation asks for.

A Schedule I or II movement out of the pharmacy for disposal, return or recall runs on a DEA Form 222 or electronic order, and the pharmacy, as the party filling that order, retains the original under 21 CFR 1305.17(b) and submits a copy to DEA at the close of the month under 21 CFR 1305.13(d).

DEA Form 41 is the record of destruction required by 21 CFR 1304.21(e) from any registered person that destroys a controlled substance under 21 CFR 1317.95(d) or causes destruction under 21 CFR 1317.95(c); it must be complete and accurate and include the name and signature of the two employees who witnessed the destruction.

A DEA Form 41 is not the record for handing stock to a reverse distributor or for transporting it to a registered location, because 21 CFR 1304.21(e) attaches the record only to the two destruction paragraphs of 21 CFR 1317.95.

The same form has a second and different use: 21 CFR 1317.05(a)(4) has a practitioner submit one copy of a DEA Form 41 to the Special Agent in Charge, listing the controlled substances it desires to dispose of, in order to request disposal assistance.

Where the Special Agent in Charge authorises a practitioner that regularly disposes of controlled substances to act without a prior application in each instance, the practitioner keeps records of those disposals and files periodic reports summarising them.

247 CMR 9.21(9) requires a pharmacy to maintain an accurate record of all controlled substances returned to a reverse distributor or disposed of in accordance with state and federal laws and regulations, including proper DEA forms in the case of Schedule II controlled substances.

The Schedule II perpetual inventory is itself a security record: it may be kept in hard copy or electronically, must reflect the amount of each Schedule II controlled substance located on the pharmacy premises, and covers each such substance the pharmacy has received, dispensed, or disposed of.

That record must include the name and strength of each Schedule II controlled substance, the quantity of each drug purchased or added to inventory, the starting inventory, prescription numbers, the dispensed quantity, the remaining balance, and pharmacist identification for each transaction.
Surveillance video is a record with its own retention rule, kept at least 14 days and at least two years where theft or diversion is known or suspected.
Documentation of pre-employment screening is retained so that it can be made available by applicants and registrants of the Department to the Commissioner upon request.

role_duties.duty: Is responsible for pharmacy security together with the pharmacist on duty, controls access to the prescription area, investigates any discrepancy found on the Schedule II reconciliation, reports any significant loss or suspected theft in accordance with federal and state requirements, and performs any inventory adjustment resulting from a discrepancy, which only a pharmacist designee acting in the Manager of Record's absence may perform instead.
May make an inventory adjustment resulting from a discrepancy in the Manager of Record's absence, and then reports the change to the Manager of Record.
May make entries into the Schedule II perpetual inventory, while an unlicensed individual may not make any entry into or adjust it.

role_duties.role: Applicant or registrant of the Department as employer
role_duties.duty: Screens new employees before employment where they may work in or around areas where controlled substances are handled, keeps the documentation available to the Commissioner on request, and does not knowingly employ any agent or employee barred by 105 CMR 700.005(B)(2).

Does not employ, as an agent or employee with access to controlled substances, anyone convicted of a felony offense relating to controlled substances or who at any time had a DEA application denied, a DEA registration revoked, or a DEA registration surrendered for cause.

Gives written notice to the Field Division Office of the Administration in its area within one business day of discovery and files a complete and accurate DEA Form 106 within 45 days, under 21 CFR 1301.76(b).

role_duties.role: Massachusetts pharmacy that has filed a DEA Form 106
role_duties.duty: Submits a copy of that form with the Report of Theft or Loss of Controlled Substance to the Board within seven days of the theft or significant loss, and files a copy simultaneously with the local police department and the department of state police.

role_duties.role: Registrant of the Department discovering theft, loss or suspected tampering
role_duties.duty: Reports to the Drug Control Program within the Department within 24 hours of discovery on the form that programme provides or approves.

role_duties.role: Retail pharmacy that contracted the carrier retrieving filled prescriptions from a central fill pharmacy
role_duties.duty: Reports in-transit losses itself on a DEA Form 106 upon discovery, under 21 CFR 1301.76(d).

role_duties.role: Supplier of a shipment lost in transit under the non-practitioner rule
role_duties.duty: Reports an in-transit loss by its agent or by the common or contract carrier it selected within one business day of discovery, except where the theft or loss occurs during an import or export transaction; this is 21 CFR 1301.74(c) and it is not the rule that governs a pharmacy's own losses.

role_duties.role: The two employees required at a destruction or transfer
role_duties.duty: Load and unload or observe the loading and unloading until a transfer is complete, accompany the substances where the registrant transports them, handle or observe the handling until the substance is rendered non-retrievable, and personally witness the destruction where 21 CFR 1317.95(c) or (d) applies.

Holds its own registration with the Administration, accepts delivery only at its registered location with personal receipt by an employee and no re-routing once en route, stores the substances under the security controls in parts 1301 and 1317, and destroys or causes the destruction of substances received for destruction no later than 30 calendar days after receipt.

role_duties.role: Registrant that destroyed or caused destruction
role_duties.duty: Maintains the DEA Form 41 record of destruction, complete and accurate, with the name and signature of the two witnessing employees.

common_traps.text: Adjusting the perpetual inventory to match a count, which resolves the paperwork and destroys the evidence; 247 CMR 9.21(8) sends a discrepancy to the Manager of Record to investigate and restricts who may make the adjustment at all.
Collapsing the two federal clocks into one, so the written notice waits for the Form 106; the notice is due within one business day of discovery and the Form 106 within 45 days after it.

Answering a Massachusetts theft or loss with the DEA filing alone, when the Board wants a copy of the Form 106 within seven days and the local and state police want copies at the moment the Form 106 is filed.
Treating the federal 45 days as the operative outer limit in Massachusetts, when the seven-day Board report requires the Form 106 much earlier.

Sending the Department's 24-hour report to the Board, or the Board's seven-day report to the Drug Control Program, when the two routes have different recipients, different instruments and different clocks.

Reading a pharmacy's federal theft-or-loss duty out of 21 CFR 1301.74(c), the non-practitioner paragraph, when 21 U.S.C. 802(21) makes a pharmacy a practitioner and 21 CFR 1301.76(b) is its paragraph; the clocks match but the sentences about recovery and in-transit losses do not travel.

Looking for a numerical threshold of significance instead of applying the factors the regulation actually lists, among them quantity in relation to the type of business, association with access by specific individuals, and any pattern of losses over a specific time period.

Reading the theft-or-loss duty in this section as covering anything other than controlled substances; the theft or loss of DEA order forms is a separate duty that belongs with the ordering rules and is not reached here.

Treating a DEA Form 41 as the receipt for anything leaving the pharmacy for disposal, when 21 CFR 1304.21(e) attaches it to destruction under 21 CFR 1317.95(d) and to causing destruction under 21 CFR 1317.95(c) and to nothing else.

Forgetting that the same form appears twice for different reasons, once as the record of a destruction and once as the copy a practitioner submits to the Special Agent in Charge to request disposal assistance.
Assuming a pharmacy may drive unwanted stock to an incinerator itself, when transport by the registrant's own means to a destruction location is written into 21 CFR 1317.05(b) for non-practitioners.
Accepting a disposal vendor on the strength of its business description or a state permit rather than confirming that it is registered with the Administration as a reverse distributor.

Believing that removing labels, crushing tablets or mixing stock into ordinary waste satisfies the destruction standard, when the substance must be rendered non-retrievable by a permanent and irreversible alteration of its physical or chemical condition.

Skipping the second employee, or having one person witness while the other only signs afterwards, when 21 CFR 1317.95 requires two employees at each stage and personal witnessing of the destruction under paragraphs (c) and (d).

Moving expired or quarantined stock out of secured storage because it can no longer be dispensed, when 247 CMR 9.21(10) applies every requirement of the section to substances that are expired, quarantined, or pending reverse distribution.

Reading the screening duty in 105 CMR 700.005(B) as an ordinary background check, when the regulation states that it is made solely to determine whether the prospective employee can be trusted to work in and around controlled substances.
Importing a look-back period into 105 CMR 700.005(B)(2), or answering it with a documented history or a notification, when its two limbs run at any time and neither device appears in the paragraph.
Applying 105 CMR 700.005(B) to a Board-licensed retail pharmacy, when it is addressed to applicants and registrants of the Department and a retail drug business registers with the Board instead.

Missing the federal bar that does reach the pharmacy, and with it the felony drug conviction and surrender-for-cause limbs, or forgetting that the federal bar turns on access to controlled substances so that the scope of a post is part of the test.

Saying that a rule stating no exception of its own admits of none, when 105 CMR 700.140 gives the Commissioner a waiver over 105 CMR 700.000 and 21 CFR 1307.03 lets any person ask DEA for an exception to a provision of the chapter.

Sending Schedule II stock to a reverse distributor with no order form, on the strength of the 21 CFR 1305.03 exception for distributions to reverse distributors, which is written for collectors and law enforcement.

Forgetting that a Schedule II return or recall has its own instrument and record under 21 CFR 1317.10, and that the pharmacy keeps the original of the order it filled and sends DEA a copy at the close of the month.
